## I Require Context

When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird .

Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can. However, LLMs are blocked on context .

Hereâs a dumb example of context growing over time:

- 1s : What

- 2s : What is

- 3s : What is le

- 4s : What is le capital

- 5s : What is le capital of

- 6s : What is le capital of France?

If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck. France is le gatekeeper , and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite. In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet .

Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken? WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty. The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU ) noticing a thing.

So thatâs what Mr. MoQ does. No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio.

Itâs not expensive either: audio is tiny . 1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets. We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact.

And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time!

The model no longer has to guess. It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either. This is a pure user experience win .

## Not Just Mics

Guess what? WebRTC doesnât just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS.

Fun Fact : WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives , not when it is supposed to be rendered . Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal. Sure, itâll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio.

This is a huge problem for voice AI . TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp. But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTCâ¦ the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet .

And if thereâs any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada.

If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet. A stamp of sorts.

## Random Access Memory

Welcome back to the future Marty . We faster than real-time now.

RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive. And being able to store stuff locally. You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers.

We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM. Absurd, I know.

Itâs how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity. MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI. Your sick baking recipe wonât be subject to surprise congestion.

And donât you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB. Youâre not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick.

Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC ?

WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio. Itâs available in every browser via libwebrtc , a C++ monolith maintained by Google. Itâs so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else.

The problem is that WebRTC is the Google Meet client . It is designed specifically for Googleâs conferencing product, not their voice AI product (they use WebSocket), and certainly not your product.

quite the anti-competitive ruse tbh . Google can ship product updates without consulting the other browser vendors. No other conferencing app can do this on the web.
